issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal after reassessing the evidence when the trial court’s view is clearly unreasonable and the appellate court gives proper weight to the considerations favoring the acquitted accused.
material_facts: The High Court reversed the trial court’s acquittal after reviewing the evidence and giving reasons for rejecting the trial court’s grounds.

The Supreme Court found that the High Court had considered the trial judge’s assessment of witness credibility, the presumption of innocence, the benefit of reasonable doubt, and the trial judge’s advantage in seeing the witnesses.
The Supreme Court found the trial court’s view clearly unreasonable and the High Court’s reasons convincing.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 417 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an appellate court has full power to review the evidence in an appeal against acquittal. It must give proper weight to the trial judge’s credibility assessments, the presumption of innocence, the accused’s entitlement to the benefit of real and reasonable doubt, and the trial judge’s opportunity to see the witnesses; it must address the reasons for acquittal and explain its decision. If two reasonable conclusions are available on the evidence, the acquittal should not be disturbed. No earlier cases are cited in the judgment.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking reversal of an acquittal.
predicates.trial_view_clearly_unreasonable: The trial court’s conclusion is clearly unreasonable on the evidence, rather than one of two reasonable conclusions.

issues.definition: When an appeal seeks reversal of an acquittal and the trial court’s view is clearly unreasonable, reversal of the acquittal is justified.

issues.legal_issue: Consistent eyewitness evidence may support a conviction when the witnesses’ account is compatible with the medical evidence, including when the account explains how the injuries occurred.
material_facts: Several eyewitnesses gave a substantially consistent account of the assault.
Three eyewitnesses had injuries that supported their presence at the scene.
The medical evidence showed multiple incised head wounds that could have been caused by the weapons described by the witnesses.
The witnesses said that kicks were delivered to the deceased’s head after the weapon blows, explaining the expulsion of brain matter.
The doctor stated that the injuries could not have been caused by a gunshot, contrary to the defence account of an accidental shooting.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no sufficient reason to reject the High Court’s assessment of the eyewitness evidence and upheld the convictions of the seven appellants whose convictions were not set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove its case independently, and reliable eyewitness evidence may be acted upon even where the witnesses are partisan. The court considered the eyewitness evidence alongside the medical evidence and rejected the defence account because the injuries were incompatible with a gunshot and the witnesses’ account explained the injuries. The convictions were under Section 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code. No earlier cases are cited in the judgment.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and eyewitness_accounts_substantially_consistent and eyewitnesses_supported_by_injuries and account_compatible_with_medical_evidence

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.eyewitness_accounts_substantially_consis: The eyewitnesses give accounts that are substantially consistent with one another.
predicates.eyewitnesses_supported_by_injuries: One or more eyewitnesses have injuries supporting their presence at the occurrence.
predicates.account_compatible_with_medical_evidence: The medical evidence is compatible with the eyewitness account, including its explanation of how the injuries occurred.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal challenges a conviction and the eyewitness accounts are substantially consistent, supported by witness injuries, and compatible with the medical evidence, the conviction is supported by the evidence.

issues.legal_issue: The benefit of reasonable doubt is due to an accused where partisan evidence attributes no injury or act of assault to that accused.
material_facts: The evidence was found to be partisan.
The first information report attributed no injury to either of the two appellants concerned and did not state that either had assaulted anyone.
The Supreme Court found the case against those two appellants was not free from reasonable doubt.
issues.conclusion: The two appellants were entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt, so their convictions were set aside and they were acquitted.
issues.legal_principle: An accused is entitled to the benefit of real and reasonable doubt. The Court applied that principle to the absence of any attributed injury or assault by the two appellants in evidence it found to be partisan. No particular statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this ruling.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.evidence_is_partisan: The evidence relied on against the accused comes from witnesses associated with an opposing party or side.
predicates.no_injury_or_assault_attributed_to_accus: The evidence does not attribute an injury or an act of assault to the accused.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal from conviction, partisan evidence that attributes no injury or assault to the accused entitles the accused to the benefit of reasonable doubt.
